references.text: Joseph is moved to tears by his meeting with his brother Benjamin and withdraws to weep, but holds himself back (ויתאפק). This is a direct precursor to 45:1, where he can no longer hold himself back (לא יכל להתאפק).
Judah's moving speech, in which he offers himself as a slave in Benjamin's place, is the direct trigger that causes Joseph to be unable to restrain his emotions any longer.
Joseph's brothers express remorse for what they did to him, and Joseph withdraws and weeps—an early sign of the feelings that ultimately lead to his revelation.
Joseph was sold by his brothers into Egypt—the background to the dramatic reunion where Joseph reveals his identity.
The Lord says he has long remained silent and held back (אתאפק), but now he will break forth—the same Hebrew root used for Joseph's self-control.
Complementary scenes showing the transition from hidden identity to full revelation in God's story of salvation.
Chronological and thematic connection: The weeping in 43:30 is the emotional precursor to the final revelation in 45:1.
Theological parallel: 'It is I' as a revelation of identity to remove fear among the brothers/disciples.
Direct narrative continuation: The revelation (v.1) is the prerequisite for the message sent to the father (v.9).
Fulfillment of prophecy: The brothers' submission in 42:6 becomes meaningful only when their identity is revealed in 45:1.
